title: Foundations of Cell and Molecular Biology
description: From molecular structure to cell behavior: build a mechanistic model of how living systems store information, capture energy, and maintain boundaries.

modifications: Normalized the course title to Foundations of Cell and Molecular Biology; the stable ID is unchanged.

outcomes.description: Use quantitative physical and biochemical models, including enzyme and free-energy relations, while checking assumptions, units, and limits.
Trace information flow from DNA to phenotype.
Interpret controls and evidence in a simple molecular experiment.

lesson_objectives.description: Distinguish covalent structure from molecular interactions.
Predict how charge, polarity, and hydrophobicity shape biomolecular assembly.
Use covalent structure and functional groups to identify chemical features that may change under a specified mutation.
Use pH relative to pKa to predict the dominant protonation state of a simple ionizable group.
Use residue environment and measurement context to make a bounded prediction about a protein substitution.
Use matched abundance, folding, and activity measurements to separate candidate mechanisms of a protein variant.
Use electrochemical gradients to determine passive ion movement.
Separate simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and active transport.
Interpret Michaelis-Menten parameters without confusing affinity and rate.
Relate ΔG to equilibrium and coupling.
Trace DNA information through transcription and translation.
Identify the purpose of positive, negative, and loading controls.
Summarize replicate-level data without turning a descriptive contrast into a causal conclusion.
Use targeting information and membrane-crossing route to predict a protein's likely destination and topology.
Interpret protease-protection and compartment-marker results with the controls needed to bound localization claims.
Trace secretory and endocytic cargo while distinguishing receptor recycling from cargo destination and membrane topology.
Use matched binding, localization, and cargo-distribution measurements to distinguish a sorting defect from altered synthesis or degradation.
Distinguish enzyme effects on activation barriers and reaction rates from effects on reaction free energy and equilibrium, and evaluate when a coupled reaction can be thermodynamically favorable.
Apply the steady-state single-substrate model to relate active-enzyme concentration, turnover, substrate concentration, Km, and initial rate while stating its assumptions.
Calculate initial rates from a specified single-substrate model and interpret apparent kinetic parameters using units and uncertainty.
Evaluate reversible-inhibition patterns and assay controls while distinguishing model consistency from proof of molecular binding mechanism.
Estimate conventional lateral resolution and sample-plane pixel size from wavelength and numerical aperture, distinguishing resolution, magnification, and contrast.
Select image controls and bound a colocalization conclusion to the spatial scale and labeling evidence measured.
Calculate marker recovery across collected fractions and distinguish enrichment from purity using a multi-marker panel.
Design fractionation controls for input, mass balance, contamination, integrity, and bounded in-cell inference.
Write an antiparallel complementary DNA strand with explicit polarity and explain how polymerase direction determines continuous and discontinuous synthesis.
Compare semiconservative, conservative, and dispersive replication predictions across controlled isotope-density generations, naming what the evidence distinguishes.
Distinguish polymerase proofreading from post-replicative mismatch repair and match lesion classes to plausible DNA repair pathways.
Evaluate synthetic lesion-removal evidence using input, perturbation, rescue, and assay controls while distinguishing lesion signal from mutation frequency.
Explain how nucleosome organization, remodeling, and context-dependent histone or DNA marks relate to chromatin accessibility without treating a mark as a transcriptional switch.
Analyze accessibility and RNA measurements across cell states, distinguish biological from technical replication, and propose a controlled perturbation of an endogenous regulatory element.
Calculate simplified ChIP-qPCR percent input and select distinct input, nonspecific-pull-down, locus-specificity, and amplification controls.
Interpret matched reporter constructs and distinguish occupancy, plasmid sequence activity, endogenous cis-regulatory causation, and direct binding.
Explain how 5-prime capping, spliceosome-mediated intron removal, alternative splicing, and 3-prime processing shape many mature eukaryotic mRNAs.
Interpret isoform-specific and shared-region RNA measurements while separating transcript production, processing, stability, and measured isoform composition.
Select perturbation, assay, and reverse-transcription controls that strengthen a bounded claim about RNA processing.
Trace eukaryotic translation initiation, elongation, and termination while preserving codon frame and peptide-growth direction.
Infer synthesis and degradation alternatives from matched RNA, nascent-protein, steady-state protein, and turnover measurements.
Apply a first-order protein-decay model to estimate half-life and state assumptions and measurement limits.
Calculate allele-transmission and phenotype probabilities under an explicit Mendelian model with stated penetrance assumptions.
Interpret pedigree evidence while distinguishing dominance, penetrance, expressivity, age, ascertainment, and sample-size limits.
Evaluate genotype-phenotype associations for linkage, population structure, environment, and causal-inference alternatives.
Map variant hypotheses across DNA, RNA, protein, cell, and organism levels while naming what each assay directly measures.
Interpret matched isogenic introduction and correction data using protein-normalized activity and viable-cell denominators.
Select independent-clone, editing, normalization, and orthogonal follow-up controls for a bounded variant-mechanism claim.
Calculate idealized single-site receptor occupancy from free ligand concentration and Kd, and distinguish binding occupancy from an operational cellular response.
Compare receptor tyrosine kinase and G-protein-coupled receptor relay logic, amplification, and context-dependent branch structure.
Interpret dose and time measurements while distinguishing receptor occupancy, biochemical state, and later cell response.
Analyze transient and sustained signaling trajectories using replicate-level measurements and stated exposure conditions.
Evaluate perturbation and bypass evidence for pathway position using target engagement and explicit inference boundaries.
Design controls and follow-up measurements that distinguish feedback, ligand availability, receptor adaptation, and intervention-specific alternatives.
Compare actin, microtubule, and intermediate-filament organization and common cellular functions while recognizing dynamic turnover and system interactions.
Trace selected integrin, cadherin, focal-adhesion, and intermediate-filament linkages without conflating cell–matrix and cell–cell junctions.
Evaluate how matrix composition, ligand presentation, and remodeling affect the interpretation of a cell–matrix experiment.
Calculate stress, strain, and a small-strain elastic modulus using compatible units, geometry, and stated material assumptions.
Interpret a matrix-modulus-associated cellular readout while distinguishing biochemical localization, traction measurement, mechanism, and cell fate.
Design matrix-mechanics controls for ligand accessibility, viscoelasticity, cell state, and force-transmission alternatives.
Relate cyclin-dependent kinase activity and selected checkpoint signals to mammalian cell-cycle transitions while distinguishing a model from direct measurement.
Distinguish DNA-content, nucleotide-incorporation, and mitotic-marker readouts and calculate a stated cell fraction or relative change with its denominator.
Evaluate a synthetic DNA-damage time course and propose controls that test cell-cycle arrest without conflating it with cell death or a single signaling mechanism.
Distinguish reversible quiescence from persistent senescence-associated arrest using longitudinal and orthogonal evidence while recognizing marker limitations.
Trace core intrinsic mitochondrial and extrinsic death-receptor routes to caspase activation and interpret apoptosis-associated measurements with their limits.
Analyze synthetic cell-state evidence and design measurements that separate reduced proliferation, senescence-associated features, apoptosis, and viable-cell loss.
Distinguish stem-cell self-renewal, differentiation, and developmental potency and compare introductory potency categories in stated contexts.
Evaluate marker, clonal, and functional evidence for a cell identity without treating a signature as proof of mature tissue function.
Identify how developmental signals, neighboring cells, extracellular matrix, and time can shape a measured lineage outcome.
Interpret a factorial cell-culture comparison while distinguishing factor-associated patterns, descriptive interaction contrasts, uncertainty, and causal claims.
Design a follow-up that controls matrix presentation and cell state and measures lineage-associated markers separately from defined function.
Bound an in-vitro regenerative-biology result and identify additional evidence and oversight needed before a clinical claim.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate scope only. Every week has original lessons except week 8, which has an ungraded cumulative practice set and is not a midterm. Weeks 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12 and 13 carry an open formative homework companion, and weeks 5, 11 and 14 carry a synthetic data-analysis lab. Planned workload is not measured, so this schedule is not evidence of semester equivalence.

weeks.title: Covalent architecture, functional groups, water, and molecular interactions
Protein sequence and structure; membranes and transport
Enzyme kinetics, free energy, and cellular energetics
Cell imaging, fractionation, and measurement limits
DNA structure, replication, repair, and genome organization
Cumulative weeks 1–7 review (ungraded practice; no midterm)
RNA processing, translation, and protein turnover
Receptors, signaling networks, feedback, and perturbation
Cytoskeleton, adhesion, extracellular matrix, and mechanobiology
Cell-cycle control, mitosis, senescence, and cell death
Development, stem-cell potency, regenerative biology, and integration

workload.basis: Not measured. Legacy nominal credit and display-time labels are not retained as workload estimates.

lessons.title: Covalent architecture, functional groups, and biological molecules
lessons.worked_example: For a cysteine-to-serine substitution, compare thiol and hydroxyl chemistry and ask whether a disulfide is plausible in the relevant compartment. If activity falls, compare soluble and insoluble fractions and include a matched wild-type control before attributing the effect to loss of disulfide formation.

lessons.title: Water, pH, and noncovalent interactions
lessons.worked_example: At pH 7.4 with pKa 6.0, the two-state acid model gives [A-]/[HA] about 25 and a protonated fraction about 0.038. Calculate the population from the ratio, then state why this solution estimate may not transfer unchanged to a folded protein whose local environment shifts pKa.

modules.title: Protein sequence, structure, and variant evidence

lessons.title: Protein sequence, structure, and variant evidence
lessons.worked_example: With a buried leucine-to-aspartate variant, destabilization is plausible, not inevitable. Compare soluble abundance, folding, and specific activity at matched protein concentration to distinguish altered stability from catalytic effects and avoid inferring a phenotype from sequence alone.

lessons.title: Membranes, transport, and electrochemical gradients
lessons.worked_example: For 5 mM K+ outside and 140 mM inside at 25 C, the ideal monovalent-ion Nernst potential is about -89 mV. At that voltage, the single-ion electrochemical terms balance even though concentrations differ; this value does not predict the whole-cell voltage or flux rate.

lessons.title: Enzymes and cellular energetics
lessons.worked_example: If [S] = Km, the model predicts v = Vmax/2. Doubling enzyme concentration doubles Vmax but leaves Km unchanged in the simple model.

lessons.title: Gene expression and experimental logic
lessons.worked_example: In a knockdown experiment, a non-targeting RNA control tests for delivery or off-target effects; a rescue with a perturbation-resistant construct strengthens causal attribution.

lessons.title: Organelle compartments, membrane topology, and protein targeting
lessons.worked_example: In synthetic protease-protection data, wild-type cargo remains protected in intact ER-derived microsomes and becomes sensitive after detergent, while a signal-deletion construct is already sensitive. Lumenal and cytosolic marker controls support the interpretation that the wild-type protein entered a membrane-enclosed compartment, without identifying which import step failed in the mutant.

lessons.title: Protein sorting, vesicle traffic, and experimental inference
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic comparison shows similar M6P-receptor ligand binding but less lysosomal delivery and more secretion for a cytosolic-tail mutant. This favors a post-binding sorting explanation but requires matched receptor abundance, fraction-recovery controls, and a rescue before stronger causal claims.

lessons.title: Homework 1 practice: trafficking, localization, and fractionation evidence (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: The lysosome-enriched cargo means are 67.75% for wild type, 42.25% for the tail mutant, and 62.50% for the motif-repaired clone. The mutant-minus-wild-type descriptive contrast is -25.50 percentage points; four independent culture preparations per group do not by themselves establish uncertainty or a molecular mechanism.

lessons.title: Enzyme catalysis, reaction mechanisms, and free energy
lessons.worked_example: For 50 nM measured active enzyme with kcat = 6 s^-1, Vmax = 300 nM s^-1 and at [S] = Km the simple model predicts v0 = 150 nM s^-1. A physically coupled pair of reactions with ΔG values +12 and -21 kJ mol^-1 has net ΔG = -9 kJ mol^-1 under those conditions; the sum alone does not show that an uncoupled cell process uses this mechanism.

lessons.title: Initial-rate evidence and reversible enzyme inhibition
lessons.worked_example: For a synthetic control with Vmax = 120 nM s^-1 and Km = 20 μM, at [S] = 40 μM the model predicts 80 nM s^-1. A competitive-like inhibitor with α = 3 predicts Km,app = 60 μM and 48 nM s^-1 at that substrate concentration. The rate pattern supports a simple model but does not prove a binding site.

lessons.title: Homework 2 practice: initial rates and reversible inhibition (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: At 40 µM substrate the vehicle mean is 80 nM·s⁻¹ and both inhibitors average 48 nM·s⁻¹. With α = 1 + 40/20 = 3 the competitive apparent Km is 60 µM, but an uncompetitive pattern can give the same 48 nM·s⁻¹ at that one concentration, so a wide substrate series is needed.

lessons.title: Cell imaging: resolution, contrast, and quantitative limits
lessons.worked_example: For 520 nm emission and NA 1.30, the ideal Rayleigh estimate is 0.61 × 520/1.30 ≈ 244 nm; a Nyquist starting point samples at about 122 nm per pixel or finer. This ideal estimate is not a guarantee for a labeled biological specimen.

lessons.title: Cell fractionation: enrichment, contamination, and recovery
lessons.worked_example: In the explicitly synthetic marker panel, 4% + 18% + 68% + 5% gives 95% ER-marker recovery. P2 contains the largest measured share of the mitochondrial marker but also substantial ER and nuclear markers; the table lacks protein and volume denominators needed for a concentration-based enrichment factor or purity claim.

modules.title: DNA structure, genome organization, and replication

lessons.title: DNA structure, genome organization, and semiconservative replication
lessons.worked_example: The template 3′-A C G T T A G C-5′ directs a complementary product 5′-T G C A A T C G-3′. After two ideal semiconservative generations in light medium, half of the DNA molecules remain hybrid and half are light; density labels distinguish molecule classes, not sequence correctness.

modules.title: DNA damage, repair, and inference from lesion assays

lessons.title: DNA damage, repair pathways, and evidence of lesion removal
lessons.worked_example: In the explicitly synthetic UV time course, initial lesion signals are comparable; after four hours, the depleted condition retains a higher signal and a matched rescue moves it toward control. This supports a factor-dependent effect in the assay, not a measured mutation rate or proof of error-free repair.

lessons.title: Homework 3 practice: replication, repair and lesion-removal evidence (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: The wild-type lesion signal remaining at 4 h averages (38 + 42 + 40 + 40) / 4 = 40%, and the repair-deficient line averages 85%. The difference is 45 percentage points. S-phase fractions are about 30% in all three lines, so unequal replication-dilution of the signal is a less likely explanation.

lessons.title: Chromatin accessibility and regulatory DNA
lessons.worked_example: Across four independent cultures per state, candidate enhancer accessibility is 78 ± 10 in state A and 19 ± 5 in state B while the gene RNA differs in the same direction. State this as an association, then propose endogenous element perturbation, matched controls, and RNA measurements before calling the enhancer causal.

lessons.title: Transcription-factor occupancy and reporter evidence
lessons.worked_example: For a 1% input aliquot with Cq 25 and a ChIP sample with Cq 22, ideal doubling gives 100 × 0.01 × 2^(25 − 22) = 8% input. This is an efficiency-dependent enrichment estimate, not an absolute molecule count or transcription rate.

lessons.title: Homework 4 practice: ChIP-qPCR percent input and matched reporters (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: The control specific-antibody mean is (6.0 + 6.4 + 5.8 + 6.2) / 4 = 6.1% input and the matched IgG mean is 0.45% input, so enrichment over IgG is 6.1 / 0.45 = 13.56-fold. The knockdown mean falls to 2.2% input. The wild-type reporter falls from 3.1 to 1.5 after knockdown while the motif-mutant reporter stays near 1.2 and 1.15.

lessons.title: RNA processing and isoform evidence
lessons.worked_example: In the synthetic depletion group, 60 skipped and 30 included isoform counts give 60/(60+30) = 66.7% skipped among the two measured forms; the shift does not establish a transcription or protein-function change.

lessons.title: Translation and protein turnover
lessons.worked_example: A background-corrected labeled protein signal that falls from 80 to 40 units over 4 hours has a 4-hour half-life under the stated first-order model; similar mRNA and half-life with lower nascent protein are consistent with reduced synthesis, not proof of a direct mechanism.

lessons.title: Homework 5 practice: mRNA, protein synthesis and turnover (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: Both lines have a mean mRNA level of 100. The variant protein level averages (52 + 48 + 50 + 50) / 4 = 50 against 100, and its nascent-protein labeling averages 50 against 100. The fraction remaining after a 4 h synthesis block is 50% in both lines, so with first-order decay the half-life is 4 h in both; the lower protein is more consistent with reduced synthesis than with faster turnover.

lessons.title: Inheritance, penetrance, and pedigree evidence
lessons.worked_example: An A/a x a/a cross transmits A with probability 1/2. At 80% penetrance by a specified age, the simplified phenotype probability is 1/2 x 0.8 = 40%; transmission and phenotype are different probabilities.

lessons.title: Variant mechanism and isogenic evidence
lessons.worked_example: Synthetic knock-in clones have about 55 Protein X units and 54 activity units per viable cell, giving 54/55 = 0.98 activity per protein unit. The lower total activity is not evidence by itself of reduced activity per molecule.

lessons.title: Homework 6 practice: penetrance and isogenic evidence (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: Penetrance among carriers is 18 / 30 = 60%, against 7 / 70 = 10% among non-carriers, so affected status is six times as frequent in carriers in this constructed table; it is an association in one dataset. In the isogenic comparison the variant line averages (41 + 44 + 39 + 40) / 4 = 41, the corrected clones 78.5 and the re-introduced variant 42.

modules.title: Receptors, signaling pathways, and network logic

lessons.title: Receptors, signaling pathways, and network logic
lessons.worked_example: At free ligand 1 nM and Kd 4 nM, idealized single-site occupancy is 1/(4+1) = 0.20. This binding estimate does not predict a 20% cell response because the equation describes binding only and omits intracellular amplification, receptor reserve, feedback, and assay-specific nonlinearities.

modules.title: Signaling dynamics, feedback, and perturbation evidence

lessons.title: Signaling dynamics, feedback, and perturbation evidence
lessons.worked_example: In the explicitly synthetic time course, pulse exposure returns phospho-ERK toward baseline while continued exposure remains elevated at 60 minutes; the readout establishes a trajectory difference, not a cell-fate outcome or a unique feedback mechanism.

modules.title: Cytoskeletal systems, adhesion, and extracellular matrix

lessons.title: Cytoskeletal systems, adhesion, and extracellular matrix
lessons.worked_example: A spreading change on fibronectin makes an integrin-linked route plausible, but an image alone cannot establish mechanism. Measure attachment, viability, accessible coating, target engagement, and the named downstream variable; then bound the claim to the tested cells and surface.

lessons.title: Matrix mechanics and mechanotransduction
lessons.worked_example: A uniform 12 μN force over 3 × 10⁻⁹ m² gives 4.0 × 10³ Pa stress. Stress is force per area; a material modulus requires the strain response over a stated range. The geometry and homogeneous-loading assumptions matter, and modulus or viscoelastic behavior requires a deformation measurement under defined conditions.

lessons.title: Homework 7 practice: matrix stiffness, controls and perturbation design (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: Mean spread area is (420 + 450 + 400 + 430) / 4 = 425 µm² on soft, 890 µm² on medium and 1490 µm² on stiff gels. The stiff-to-soft ratio is 1490 / 425 = 3.51. Cell density (about 140 to 150 per mm²) and relative ligand density (about 100) are matched, so those two alternatives are reduced, but gel stiffness is a stand-in for several properties and the readout is one cell shape measure.

lessons.title: Cell-cycle control, checkpoints, and mitosis
lessons.worked_example: A 20-minute EdU pulse labels 60 of 240 viable singlets: 60/240 = 25% of the gated population incorporated nucleotide during the pulse. This does not identify the exact cell-cycle duration or prove which checkpoint pathway acted.

modules.title: Quiescence, senescence, apoptosis, and cell-fate evidence

lessons.title: Quiescence, senescence, apoptosis, and cell-fate evidence
lessons.worked_example: Low EdU after stress supports reduced DNA synthesis in the sampled cells, not a unique cell-state diagnosis. Rechallenge, orthogonal arrest and damage markers, caspase measurements, and viable-cell recovery answer separate questions and need explicit denominators.

lessons.title: Homework 8 practice: quiescence, senescence and cell-state markers (open, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: Both arrested states have a low DNA-synthesis label (5% and 4% against 40% in proliferating cells), so that marker alone does not separate them. The stress-associated enzyme marker is 9% in the serum-withdrawn cultures and 65% in the damage-induced cultures. After stimulation, re-entry averages 34% for the quiescent cultures and 6% for the damage-induced cultures, a 28 percentage-point difference.

modules.title: Developmental potency, stem-cell states, and lineage evidence

lessons.title: Developmental potency, stem-cell states, and lineage evidence
lessons.worked_example: Eighteen of 80 recovered viable constructs meet a predeclared stimulation-response threshold: 18/80 × 100% = 22.5%. This is the fraction of recovered constructs meeting that assay threshold, not proof of a mature tissue or clinical benefit.

lessons.title: Integrative regenerative-biology study design
lessons.worked_example: The synthetic cue-associated difference is 38−12 = 26 percentage points at 2 kPa and 63−24 = 39 points at 30 kPa; the descriptive difference-in-differences is 13 points. Batch-level uncertainty still requires the underlying independent-batch values and a prespecified model.

modules.title: Virtual laboratory: quantitative fluorescence image analysis

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: quantitative fluorescence image analysis
lessons.worked_example: The four synthetic vehicle batch fractions average to 13 percent; the four cue fractions average to 22 percent. Their descriptive difference is 9 percentage points. Four preparations, not the 800 sampled nuclei, are the independent replicate count per condition.

modules.title: Virtual laboratory: signaling dynamics, inhibition, and rescue

lessons.title: Virtual lab 2: signaling time course, controls, and rescue
lessons.worked_example: At 2 minutes, mean relative pERK is 4.90 under continuous ligand and 1.15 with MEK inhibitor. Subtracting vehicle (1.00) gives 3.90 and 0.15 above baseline; the observed residual fraction is 0.15/3.90 = 3.85%. This synthetic comparison measures one downstream phosphorylation readout and does not establish inhibitor specificity or a later cell outcome.

modules.title: Virtual laboratory: lineage-marker time course and state inference

lessons.title: Virtual lab 3: lineage-marker time course and state inference
lessons.worked_example: At day 8 the factor condition averages (58 + 60 + 57 + 59) / 4 = 58.5% lineage-marker-positive cells against 7.5% in control, a 51 percentage-point difference. Cells per well average 241 thousand with the factor and 451 thousand in control, so the factor condition has fewer cells: a rise in the marker fraction can reflect conversion of cells, selective loss or slower growth of marker-negative cells, or a mix. The marker-positive cells per well are about 141 thousand (0.585 × 241) with the factor against about 34 thousand (0.075 × 451) in control, so the marker-positive count also rises, which a fraction alone cannot show.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: Learners may request one human review per attempt; operator-provisioned reviewers can decide only when the installed question specification matches the saved attempt. This workflow does not provide course-level human grading.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The package uses text-described route sequences and tables; no source figures are imported. Future original diagrams require concise descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.
